reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Presents as well-demarcated, chalk-white macules and patches with complete loss of pigment, typically symmetrical in the common non-segmental form
Favoured sites include periorificial areas (around the eyes and mouth), the hands, and other acral and extensor surfaces
Wood's lamp examination accentuates the depigmented patches and helps detect early or subtle lesions, especially in lighter skin
New patches may appear at sites of trauma or friction (Koebner phenomenon)
As an autoimmune condition, it is associated with other autoimmune diseases, particularly thyroid disease, so consider screening for these
Management options include topical corticosteroids and calcineurin inhibitors, phototherapy for more extensive disease, and rigorous photoprotection of depigmented skin
The psychosocial impact can be substantial, particularly in darker skin and in visible areas, and should be addressed directly
Set realistic expectations: repigmentation is slow and variable, and hair-bearing and facial areas respond better than acral sites
reference.pathophysiology: Vitiligo is an acquired disorder characterised by immune-mediated destruction of epidermal melanocytes, leading to loss of pigment. Current understanding emphasises an interplay of genetic susceptibility, intrinsic melanocyte vulnerability with oxidative stress, and an autoimmune response in which CD8 cytotoxic T cells and interferon-gamma signalling target and destroy melanocytes. The absence of functioning melanocytes leaves affected skin devoid of melanin, producing the characteristic depigmented macules. Non-segmental vitiligo tends to be symmetrical and progressive with autoimmune associations, whereas segmental vitiligo is localised to a dermatomal-like distribution and often stabilises after an early active phase.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis aided by Wood's lamp examination
Thyroid function tests and thyroid autoantibodies given autoimmune associations
Screening for other autoimmune disease when clinically indicated
Skin biopsy only in atypical cases to confirm melanocyte loss
Assessment of disease activity and extent to guide and monitor therapy
redFlags: Rapidly spreading depigmentation indicating active, unstable disease
A solitary hypopigmented patch with reduced sensation, which should prompt exclusion of leprosy where endemic
Symptoms suggesting associated autoimmune disease, such as thyroid dysfunction
Significant psychological distress warranting mental health support
reference.prognosis: Vitiligo follows an unpredictable course; spontaneous repigmentation is uncommon and treatment results are variable, with facial and truncal lesions generally more responsive than acral and hair-bearing sites. It is not physically dangerous but can be psychologically distressing and often chronic.
pitfalls: Confusing it with pityriasis versicolor or post-inflammatory hypopigmentation
Failing to protect depigmented skin from sunburn and photodamage
Underestimating the psychological burden and promising unrealistic repigmentation
management: Topical corticosteroids and topical calcineurin inhibitors as first-line therapy to arrest progression and promote repigmentation
Topical JAK inhibitor (ruxolitinib) for non-segmental facial and limited disease
Narrowband ultraviolet B phototherapy for extensive or progressive disease, with targeted excimer light for localised patches
Rigorous photoprotection of depigmented skin and cosmetic camouflage to reduce contrast
Surgical melanocyte or epidermal grafting for stable segmental disease, and depigmentation therapy in extensive refractory cases
Screen for and manage associated autoimmune disease, particularly thyroid dysfunction
Psychological support for the distress and impact on quality of life, with dermatology referral
